{{< include _head.qmd >}}

Pick the mode of the starting key, the mode of the key it ends in, and how far apart the two tonics are, counted in half steps up
from the first tonic (7 half steps: C major to G major, or A minor to E minor). The bars show how many examples there are at each
distance; click one to list them. Each result shows the whole path of keys the analysis names, and plays like the scores on the book
pages. How to read the labels: [Analysed Scores](index.qmd#reading-the-labels).

There are two kinds of example. The **textbook** ones are written to show a modulation, a few chords long. The **real pieces** are
short passages, two bars before a key change to three after, from Bach's four-part chorales and from 19th-century songs; their
headings give the bars, and the link opens the full analysis.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For teachers

- **Which keys count:** the start is the example's first key and the end its last, as the book's title names them where it does
  (Reger, Rimsky-Korsakov, Tchaikovsky and the textbooks' own progressions); otherwise the analysis's first and last keys. An example that
  goes out and comes back (Kostka 19-4, C → E♭ → G♭ → C) counts as 0 half steps; its path shows where it went.
- **Distance** is counted up from the first tonic, so 7 is a 5th up or a 4th down. Enharmonic keys count the same (C to D♭ and C to C♯
  are both 1).
- **Data:** the textbook examples are written by `scripts/when-in-rome/build.mjs` with the book pages, so they always match them
  (Reger's example 41 has no notes in the corpus and is left out). The passages from real pieces are written by
  `scripts/when-in-rome/corpus.mjs` to `apps/shared/data/modulation-corpus.json`, loaded after the page shows.
- **Which key changes become passages:** the old key lasted at least 2 bars and the new one lasts at least 2, so a chord or two
  tonicizing a key is not counted; at most 2 a piece. A passage is kept only if the analysis fits its notes: at three quarters or
  more of the numerals, at least two of the chord's notes are sounding. That threw out the passages whose bar numbers did not line up.
- **Analysts differ:** the chorales are Dmitri Tymoczko's analyses, which name a new key at most cadences; the songs are by
  contributors to the *Working in Harmony* app, proof-read by Mark Gotham. Some keys they name, a teacher might call a tonicization.
- **Left out of the songs:** the words, and grace notes.
:::

**For students**

Gotham, Mark, et al. *When in Rome: A Meta-Corpus of Functional Harmony*. GitHub. [github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome](https://github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome). The analyses on this page (RomanText files), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Hutchinson, Robert. "Modulation." *Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*, ch. 22, U of Puget Sound. [musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Modulation.html](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Modulation.html). Tonicization against modulation, closely related keys, diatonic and chromatic pivot chords, and direct, common-tone and sequential modulation.

OpenScore. *OpenScore Lieder Corpus*. GitHub. [github.com/OpenScore/Lieder](https://github.com/OpenScore/Lieder). The songs' notes (MusicXML, CC0), from which the finder's song passages are cut and the library's songs are drawn; the words are left out.

Sapp, Craig Stuart, encoder. *370 Four-part Chorales by J. S. Bach in the Humdrum File Format*. GitHub. [github.com/craigsapp/bach-370-chorales](https://github.com/craigsapp/bach-370-chorales). The chorale's notes (after Dörffel's edition, Breitkopf & Härtel, c. 1875), converted to ABC for this page.

Tymoczko, Dmitri, analyst. Roman-numeral analyses of the Bach chorales and of Beethoven, Piano Sonata Op. 27 No. 2, in *When in Rome*. [github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome/tree/master/Corpus](https://github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome/tree/master/Corpus). The chorale's analysis; his readings of the Moonlight are quoted where they differ from Chen and Su's.

**For teachers**

Nápoles López, Néstor, et al. *Key Modulation Dataset*. GitHub (DDMAL). [github.com/DDMAL/key_modulation_dataset](https://github.com/DDMAL/key_modulation_dataset). The encodings and analyses of the textbook examples, translated to RomanText by Nápoles López and copied into When in Rome.

*Working in Harmony* (app). Fourscore and More. [fourscoreandmore.org/apps/working-in-harmony/](https://fourscoreandmore.org/apps/working-in-harmony/). Where the song analyses in When in Rome were made, by contributors, and proof-read by Mark Gotham.
